name: TrackingTime
tagline: Timer and timesheet app for tracking hours against clients, projects and tasks, with team reports and billable rates.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Time tracking is one of the most solved-in-an-afternoon problems in SaaS: a start/stop button, a projects table, a duration sum and a CSV export. For one person tracking their own billable hours, an agent can produce something genuinely usable in a session, and you get to define the fields your invoices actually need. Where TrackingTime earns money is everything around the timer: native mobile and desktop apps, a browser extension that nudges you when you forget, dozens of integrations that let a task in Asana or Jira become a time entry, and manager-facing reports across a team. None of that is the core loop, all of it is real work. If you are a solo freelancer who mostly forgets to hit start, the DIY version fails in exactly the same place the paid one does.
coreLoopDIY: A local web app where you start and stop a timer against a client, project and task, edit or add entries by hand, and export a filtered timesheet as CSV with billable totals.
requirements: Node 20+ and a machine you leave running, or a small VPS
A browser you keep a tab pinned in
Willingness to hit start yourself, since there is no extension nagging you
whatYouLose: Native iOS and Android apps, so tracking away from your desk means remembering to backfill
Integrations with project tools, so no turning a Jira ticket into a time entry with one click
The browser extension and idle detection that catch the sessions you forgot to start
Team views: who is working on what, approvals, manager reports
Invoicing and payroll exports that downstream tools already understand
moatNotes: The moat is not the stopwatch, it is being present on every device and inside every tool where work actually starts.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because time tracking only works if it is frictionless, and friction lives in the last mile. People pay for the phone app, the browser nag, the one-click start from inside the task manager they already live in, and for a manager to be able to see the week without chasing anyone. A solo consultant with three clients and a spreadsheet habit can absolutely replace this. A five person studio that needs approvals and billable rate reports will spend more time maintaining the DIY version than the subscription costs.
notes: The stopwatch is trivial; the discipline is not, and no software fixes that for you.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal time tracking app. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js 15 App Router with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/time.db, schema created on first run
- Tailwind CSS, no component library
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost, single user, no auth

Data model:
- clients: id, name, default_hourly_rate, archived
- projects: id, client_id, name, hourly_rate (nullable, falls back to client rate), billable (bool), color, archived
- entries: id, project_id, description, started_at, ended_at (nullable while running), tags (comma string)

Features, in scope:
1. Header timer bar: pick a project, type a description, hit start. Big running elapsed clock, stop button. Only one entry may run at a time; starting a new one stops the current one.
2. Today view: list of today's entries grouped by project, inline editable description, start and end times, and project. Delete with confirm.
3. Week view: a 7 column grid of days by project with per-cell hours, row totals, column totals, and a week grand total. Arrow keys to move weeks.
4. Manual entry: add a past entry by date, start, end, or by duration in "1h 30m" format.
5. Reports page: filter by date range, client, project, billable flag. Show total hours, billable hours, and computed amount using the rate fallback. Group by project or by day.
6. CSV export of the current filtered report: date, client, project, description, start, end, hours, rate, amount.
7. Settings page to manage clients and projects, set rates, archive things.
8. Persist a running timer across page reloads and server restarts by reading it from the DB, never from browser state.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile apps, browser extensions, idle detection, third party integrations, invoicing PDFs, multi user, approvals.

Rules: all durations stored as UTC timestamps and rendered in local time. Round only at display time, never in storage. Include a seed script with two clients and four projects so the UI is not empty. Any config goes in .env with a committed .env.example. Write a README with setup, backup instructions (just copy the db file), and a note on how to add a rate override.
